Based on the healthcare Q&A matches provided, it appears that p53 alterations are not a useful predictor of tumor response to pre-operative chemotherapy and radiotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer.

While some patients with mutated p53 (those diagnosed with mutations in the TP53 gene) may respond better or differently to certain treatments, the evidence suggests that p53 alterations detected by immunohistochemical (IHC) or single-stranded conformation polymorphism analysis (SSCP) analysis are not clinically useful predictors of local response to pre-operative adjuvant therapy in advanced rectal carcinoma.

In fact, the Q&A matches highlight the following key points:

* A study found that p53 alteration detected by IHC or SSCP analysis is not a predictive factor for tumor response to pre-operative chemotherapy and radiotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer.
* Another study suggests that patients with mutated p53 (those who received radiation therapy) may have worse outcomes than those without mutations, but this finding was only observed in the context of pelvic exenteration for recurrent rectal cancer.

These findings indicate that while p53 alterations may be relevant in certain contexts or patient populations, they are not a reliable predictor of response to pre-operative chemotherapy and radiotherapy in locally advanced rectal cancer.
